chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, in the wisdom of the progeny of Dawud (peace be upon him): It is befitting for the intellectual Muslim that he is not seen traveling/moving except for three [purposes]: restoration of his livelihood, or provision for his Hereafter, or pleasure in that which is not forbidden.

And it is befitting for the intellectual Muslim that he has an hour in which he devotes himself to his affairs between himself and Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and an hour in which he meets his brethren, with whom he exchanges advice and they exchange advice with him regarding the matters of their Hereafter; and an hour in which he leaves his soul and its pleasures in that which is not forbidden, for indeed these are an aid upon those two hours.

key_terms.حِكْمَةِ آلِ دَاوُدَ: Wisdom of the progeny of Dawud

ai.seo_question: How should a Muslim divide their time according to the wisdom of the progeny of Dawud?
ai.summary: Attributed to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), this hadith codifies the Shia concept of 'al-hal al-thalatha' (the three states), balancing worldly duties, spiritual devotion, and permissible leisure to prevent burnout and moral decay. It reflects the Imams' pragmatic approach to human nature, where rest is not merely idleness but a necessary sustenance for sustained worship and social engagement. This tripartite division underscores the holistic Islamic view of life, integrating material, spiritual, and psychological well-being.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Al Hakam, from Muhammad Bin Sama’at, from Muhammad Bin Marwan, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘It is in the wisdom of the progeny of Dawood<sup>as</sup>: ‘It is befitting for the intellectual Believer that he does not see the transitory except regarding three (matters) – Restoration of his livelihood, or provision for his Hereafter, or a pleasure in other than with Prohibitions.

And it is befitting for the intellectual Muslim that there happens to be for him a time dedicated to his affairs in what is between him and Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Mighty and Majestic, and a time (dedicated to) meeting his brethren whom he advises them and they advise him regarding the matters of the Hereafter, and a time (dedicated) to be alone to himself, and its pleasures in other than the Prohibitions, for these are an aid upon those two times (the first two)’.
en.sarwar: 1. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Muhammad ibn Sanaa ‘ah from Muhammad ibn Marwan who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘

It is in the wisdom of Ale (family) Dawud that a reasonable Muslim should not travel unless it is for three kinds of tasks: amending one’s means of living, supplies for the hereafter or enjoyment with lawful matters.

A reasonable Muslim should assign certain hours of his time to work on the matters between him and Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, certain hours to meet his brothers (in belief) with whom he speaks and they speak with him about the issues of the hereafter, and certain hours for himself and matters of enjoyment with lawful matters which are helpful during these two hours.”
